post.title: Different and the new marketing operating model
post.body:
Different puts a broader marketing operating model on display: AI participating beyond asset creation, closer to campaign operations.

Different emerged from stealth on October 20, 2026 with $48 million in funding, according to its announcement. The company says its platform builds work across advertising, email, landing pages, and AEO content, then connects creation with activation, measurement, and resource reallocation. Marketers review, direct, and approve the work. The launch materials do not define the boundaries around activation or budget changes.

Different illustrates one possible operating model. It does not prove a market-wide shift. Its product claims have not been independently tested, and the launch materials leave out pricing, complete channel and integration coverage, attribution methodology, security architecture, permission design, and detailed budget controls.

For marketers, that changes the job:

- Teams move from reviewing assets to supervising workflows. Decide what AI can initiate, which systems it can access, and when a person must intervene.

- Governance becomes part of campaign design. Set permissions, approval paths, and stop conditions before an agent enters production.

- Measurement becomes an operating input. If performance data influences the next action or resource decision, attribution quality affects execution as well as reporting.

The takeaway: design how AI participates in marketing work before choosing a product. Evaluate any system by how clearly it defines roles, controls, and measurement.

Where would your team need a human checkpoint in an AI-supported campaign workflow?

post.title: Zoom and the marketing value of shared customer context
post.body:
Customer context is about to have more readers. That gives it more chances to be wrong.

On October 20, Zoom announced a Unified Context Layer that brings together signals from customer engagements, transcripts, CRM data, and live conversations for human and AI agents. Availability varies through early 2027; Zoom calls dates estimates, subject to change.

Zoom says shared context helps businesses understand customer needs and put conversations in context across interactions. The catch: when every agent reads the same context, one wrong entry no longer misleads a single rep. It misleads them all at once.

That context can give marketers explanations clickstreams may not. Clicks show what customers did. Conversations can help explain why.

Picture a hypothetical: support calls keep surfacing the same pricing objection, traced to one claim on one landing page. Conversation context may reveal explanations behavioral data alone does not.

Three places to start:

- **Trace friction to its source.** Link recurring questions, objections, and failed handoffs to preceding campaigns.
- **Build from what customers tell you.** Let stated preferences shape segments and messaging, with permission confirmed.
- **Watch the physical channel.** Zoom says kiosks can capture product interest and promotional feedback, intent signals it describes as historically available through digital channels.

The takeaway: unified context can turn conversations into journey intelligence. The advantage goes to teams that connect what customers say to marketing changes, vet sources, and correct the record.

What would your customers' conversations explain that your journey data can't?

post.title: TapClicks MCP and the gap between access and trust
post.body:
Letting AI reach your marketing data is easy. Trusting its answer in front of a client is a separate decision.

On October 22, 2026, TapClicks released TapClicks MCP. MCP is a connector that lets AI assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini ask questions of approved marketing data in TapClicks, without manual spreadsheet exports. TapClicks says it is available on Smart packages, with usage limits that vary by package.

TapClicks says each person signs in with their own login, and the connection inherits existing client and data permissions. The company says it checks access on every request and logs those requests. It also says the assistant checks which data is available before searching and reports when a requested number does not exist.

Those controls limit what someone can reach. They do not prove an answer is correct, complete or ready for a client report or spending decision.

Before an answer leaves your team, settle three things:

- **Set the boundary.** An internal summary may be fine; client reports and spending recommendations need review.
- **Check the numbers.** A person should compare important figures with the original TapClicks data.
- **Keep your own record.** TapClicks logs requests, but your team should record who asked, which client data was available, what came back and who approved its use.

The takeaway: Login permissions govern access. Your team still decides whether an answer is sound enough to use.

Who signs off before an AI answer reaches your clients?

post.title: Facebook's Your Algorithm controls
post.body:
Facebook just gave users a steering wheel for its recommendation engine. Marketers should pay attention.

Meta's new "Your Algorithm" controls let users tell Facebook what they want to see more or less of across Feed and Reels. People can also set temporary topic interests, and Facebook says those choices will directly shape future recommendations.

This is bigger than a settings update. It is another step away from passive, black-box feeds and toward recommendation systems that users can actively train.

For marketers, that changes the job:

- Specificity beats broad reach. If users can explicitly choose topics, generic content becomes easier to tune out. Clear subject matter and a recognizable point of view matter more.

- Audience intent gets more visible. Topic controls can create stronger interest clusters, giving relevant content a better chance to find the right people, not merely the largest audience.

- Creative fatigue gets punished faster. "Not interested" is becoming a direct product input. Repetitive formats and bait-and-switch hooks may lose distribution more quickly.

The takeaway: don't build a content strategy around pleasing an algorithm you cannot see. Build one around being chosen by the people who can now help train it.

If your audience could directly tune your brand in or out, what would make them ask for more?

post.title: Google AI Mode ads and Personal Intelligence
post.body:
Google is testing what happens when search ads meet personal context. Marketers should pay attention.

Search Engine Land reports that Google has started testing ads in AI Mode for users who opt in to Personal Intelligence, which can connect Search to Gmail, Google Calendar, and Google Photos. The ads may reflect the query, the AI-generated response, user interests, and limited insights or summaries from connected apps. Advertisers cannot access those apps, and Google has not announced new controls, targeting options, or a wider rollout.

This goes beyond adding another ad slot. AI Mode can tailor answers using context such as past purchases, hobbies, preferred brands, and dining preferences. An ad may now appear beside an answer shaped around one person's situation.

For marketers, that changes the job:

- Relevance gets judged in context. Generic copy may feel especially out of place beside an answer tailored to one person.

- Query data may explain less. Watch for performance patterns that keywords alone do not account for, without assuming new reporting tools exist.

- Trust belongs in the creative brief. Personal Intelligence is opt-in, and Google says personalization can make mistakes. An ad that feels intrusive can undermine the experience around it.

The takeaway: do not wait for new targeting buttons. Prepare for search ads to be judged by how well they fit someone's situation, not only the phrase they typed.

If your ad appeared inside a personalized answer, would it feel helpful or invasive?

post.title: ChatGPT Ads and the hidden targeting path
post.body:
ChatGPT Ads puts a new wrinkle in the new media landscape: can your team spend confidently on targeting it can't fully inspect?

On October 21, 2026, OpenAI described its ad system. In chats eligible to show ads, OpenAI says a trained AI model follows the current conversation and finds possible ads. A separate auction process evaluates those candidates, chooses what runs, and handles pricing. If a user turns on ad personalization, the system may also use details from earlier chats that OpenAI classifies as not sensitive.

That creates a visibility gap. OpenAI's article does not say advertisers receive the conversation, the AI's summary, or the full path behind the choice. Exactly what advertisers can inspect remains unclear.

Digiday reported mixed experiences. Some ad buyers had problems matching clicks and sales or getting timely reports. Others said their click totals matched. The sources reviewed include no independent check of how the system works, and they do not prove better ad relevance, sales, or return on spending.

For any team testing ads based on conversations:

- Ask the person responsible for privacy to approve how the test uses guesses drawn from conversations.
- Compare sales reported by the platform with your company's own sales records.
- Set targets before the test, then increase spending only if the results meet them.

The takeaway: when you can see less of how an ad was chosen, you need stronger checks before spending more.

What evidence would your team require before increasing the budget?
